summary:
The lunar South Pole is a major focus of NASA’s Artemis programme because its permanently shadowed craters may contain water ice. However, its extreme temperatures, steep terrain, limited sunlight and loose surface dust make it a challenging environment for future lunar missions. To prepare for these conditions, space agencies use Earth-based analog sites to study and simulate different lunar environments. However, information about these sites is scattered across scientific papers and agency publications, making it difficult to find suitable locations and compare them with the Moon.

To address this problem, Where on Earth is the Moon is developed as a free, browser-based mapping platform that brings information about 87 Earth-based analog sites together in one place. The sites are organised into eight topics and categorised according to the mission activities they support, including mobility, drilling, habitat and navigation. The platform also includes a comparison module to evaluate how closely each site resembles a lunar location, four environmental data layers, and a 3D lunar map featuring 22 verified features using NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter imagery. Users can also submit, vote on and discuss potential analog sites through the community module.

Overall, the platform provides an accessible reference for students, researchers and engineers to explore and compare lunar analog sites, supporting education and preparation for future lunar missions.
details:
What it does

Where on Earth is the Moon is a free, browser-based map that matches real Earth sites to the conditions of the lunar South Pole. It holds 87 Earth sites sorted into eight topics (geology, minerals, terrain and craters, slope, temperature and sunlight, ice and permafrost, lava tubes, and planetary analogs). Each site is tagged with the tasks it supports, such as mobility, drilling, habitat and navigation. A Compare tab puts any site beside a lunar reference like Shackleton crater and rates each row Close, Partly or Different. It always states what stays different, like gravity and air. Four live layers (temperature, slope, sunlight and wind erosion) are calculated from open data. A 3D Moon built from NASA LRO imagery shows 22 verified features. Users can also sign in with Google to add, vote on and discuss new candidate sites.

Benefits and intended impact

Information about analog sites is scattered across scientific papers and agency pages. Our platform brings it together so students, engineers and researchers can quickly see which Earth site suits a task and how closely it matches the Moon. We hope it supports early-stage Artemis planning, education and public engagement.

Tools and technology

The project is a single HTML page that runs in any browser. It uses Leaflet for the 2D map, Three.js for the 3D Moon, and Firebase (Cloud Firestore and Google sign-in) for shared places, votes and comments. Data comes from NASA Moon Trek (LRO WAC and LOLA), the IAU Gazetteer, Open-Meteo, AWS Terrain Tiles, NOAA solar equations, Esri imagery, and Wikipedia and OpenStreetMap.

What makes it creative

Instead of only listing sites, we score how well each Earth site matches the Moon and show where it doesn't. The community feature lets anyone help grow the map, with points and ranks to encourage them.

Factors we considered

We put a source tag on every figure. We label simplified models (the erosion and temperature layers) as such, and we label community pins as unreviewed, flagging them after three reports. Only a nickname and avatar are public, and emails are never shown. Next steps are verified badges for community pins, moderation, more analog sites and a mobile layout review.
dataRefs: NASA LRO Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA)
NASA LCROSS (Lunar Crater Observation and Sensing Satellite)
